transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, hello Doctor. Um... yes, well, I suppose I'm here because of the historical society project. I just sort of took it on like I could run the whole fundraiser all by myself, you know? I started drawing up all these intricate quilt designs... which, oh, reminds me, I found this absolutely stunning vintage calico at an estate sale a few months ago. It has these tiny little yellow daisies on it. My grandmother used to have an apron with almost the exact same pattern when I was a little girl growing up in Ohio. The summers there were just so humid, nothing like here... but anyway, the fabric was just perfect. 

So I was calling all the volunteers, making these huge schedules for everyone, and promising all these deadlines for the quilts that I couldn't possibly meet. I just kept saying yes to everything. But really, you can't find good cotton like that anymore, it's all synthetic blends now at the craft stores. My daughter hates the synthetic stuff too, she says it makes her skin itch. 

Wait... I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, why I'm here. Yes, the fundraiser just got to be a bit much, I suppose.
Lately, have you been feeling down, sad, or have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose... it's just been hard lately. I used to absolutely love checking my garden every single morning, and working on my own quilt entries. The county fair is usually my favorite time of year. Oh, the fair back in Ohio was just spectacular, though. They had this enormous Ferris wheel, and they sold these funnel cakes that were dusted with so much powdered sugar you'd look like a ghost after eating one. My ex-husband bought me one on our first anniversary. He was wearing this navy blue sweater, which was just a terrible choice for powdered sugar, let me tell you. I tried to brush it off his chest and just made a huge white smear. He was always so particular about his clothes, taking them to the dry cleaners every Tuesday... 

But, oh, what was I saying? Right, the quilting and the garden. Lately, I just look at the fabric and the seed catalogs that come in the mail, and I feel nothing much at all. Just sort of... blank. Which is a shame because the new catalogs have some lovely heirloom tomatoes this year. My neighbor grew heirlooms last summer, huge lumpy things, but they tasted wonderful on a sandwich with a little mayonnaise and salt. I think she uses a special fertilizer, but she won't tell anyone what it is.
Can you tell me more about how often you've been feeling this way, and whether you've noticed it affecting other areas of your life, like your sleep, appetite, or energy levels?

Well, let's see... it's been about nine months now. Ever since the quilt orders fell behind and all those dreadful conflicts with the volunteers blew up, I’ve just been stuck in this low, guilty place. It was mostly Mary and Susan who started the arguing, you see. They got into this huge spat over the binding on the star pattern quilts. Susan insists on doing a bias binding, which, well, it does look neater if you have curved edges, but we were doing straight edges! My mother always told me bias binding was just a complete waste of good fabric unless you're making a scalloped hem. She made my sister this beautiful scalloped dress for Easter once back in 1974. Pastel pink with little white pearl buttons. Oh, it rained so hard that Easter, the mud got all over her shoes before we even made it up the church steps... 

But, oh, you asked about my sleep and energy, didn't you? Yes, my energy is just gone. I mostly just lie in bed... though my mattress is getting terribly lumpy on the left side, actually. I bought it at Macy's during a Labor Day sale maybe ten years ago? Or was it Memorial Day? They always have those big white sales with the red and blue balloons tied to the bedposts in the showroom. You know, I wonder if I should just flip the mattress over. Do they even make double-sided mattresses anymore? My daughter told me they mostly just make the ones with the pillow-top on one side now so you can't flip them. Which just seems like a sneaky way to make you buy a new one faster, doesn't it?
You mentioned feeling this way for about nine months. Have you had continuous symptoms without any significant relief during this time?

Well, yes, I suppose it's been pretty constant. Ever since those quilt orders fell behind and all the arguing with the volunteers really blew up, I've just been stuck in this low, guilty place for the whole nine months. No real breaks from it, just... heavy. 

Which is really a shame, because usually around month six of any big project, I'd be planning the celebration dinner. I used to make this incredible pot roast for the volunteer appreciation dinner. The secret is to sear the meat in a cast iron skillet first, and you have to use a really good cut of chuck roast. I always went to this little butcher shop downtown, right next to where the old hardware store used to be. Oh, the hardware store closed down a few years ago... they put in one of those fancy coffee shops with the baristas who wear the little beanies and the aprons that look like leather. I went in there once and asked for a regular cup of coffee, just black, and they looked at me like I had two heads! They had all these little chalkboards with words like 'macchiato' and 'flat white.' My daughter drinks those flat whites. She says the milk is steamed differently, but honestly, milk is milk, isn't it? I remember when the milkman used to deliver it right to our front porch in those heavy glass bottles... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the nine months. Yes, it's just been a continuous sort of sadness since the whole fundraiser mess happened.
During these nine months of feeling down, have you had any periods where your mood improved significantly, even for just a few days?

Well, no, not during these nine months... but right before all this started, I did have a few weeks where things were quite different. I felt almost glowing, you know? Like every single idea I had was just wonderful. I had all these grand plans for the quilt show, and I felt so... bright. But then, if anyone questioned me, I got terribly snappish. I acted like they were just standing in my way. Which is exactly what happened with Susan and that bias binding. I told her we were doing straight edges, and she just kept pushing, and I snapped at her right in front of everyone. 

I don't usually snap at people, really. Well, except maybe my ex-husband when he would leave his wet towels on the bathroom floor. He had this awful habit of just dropping them right there after his shower. And they were these heavy, dark green towels that took forever to dry. We bought them at JCPenney when they were having a home goods sale. They had this beautiful display in the store window with a faux marble bathtub and these little decorative soaps shaped like seashells. I bought a box of those soaps, actually, but they were so pretty I never wanted to use them. They just sat in a little glass dish on the counter collecting dust for years. I think I finally threw them out when we moved. Moving is such a dreadful chore, isn't it? All those boxes... 

But, oh, right, the mood. Yes, I was feeling so wonderful and glowing right before the crash, but very irritable if people didn't go along with my ideas.
Before you started feeling down, did you have a time when you felt unusually high, overly energetic, or so good that you didn’t feel like you needed much sleep?

Well, yes, exactly. During that glowing time I was telling you about, right before everything fell apart, I was hardly sleeping at all. I'd maybe get a few hours of rest, and then I'd just pop right out of bed, completely ready to go. I'd be up at all hours sewing those quilt blocks or making phone calls to coordinate the fundraiser. 

I remember calling poor Mrs. Higgins at 5:00 in the morning once. She's the one who makes those lovely lemon bars for the bake sale every year. Have you ever had a really good lemon bar? You have to get the shortbread crust just right, or it gets all soggy underneath the lemon curd. My grandmother used to make them with Meyer lemons from her own tree in the backyard. That tree was huge, it shaded the whole patio. We used to sit out there on wrought iron chairs... you know, the kind that leave those little crosshatch marks on the back of your legs if you wear shorts? I wore these bright yellow shorts one summer, probably around 1982, and I sat on that chair for so long reading a romance novel that I had marks on my legs for three days. 

But... oh, you were asking about my sleep, weren't you? Yes, back then I barely needed any sleep and felt fantastic. But now? Now it's just awful. I either lie awake in the dark just worrying and fretting about the volunteers and the quilt orders, or I end up sleeping terribly late into the morning. And even when I do sleep late, I still wake up feeling completely worn out. Just exhausted, right down to my bones.

Before you started feeling down, did you have a period lasting several days or more where you felt so good that you thought you didn’t need much sleep, or where you were much more talkative, active, or easily distracted than usual?

Yes, yes, exactly. During that... that glowing time before the crash, I was so talkative, it was like I couldn't get the words out fast enough. In our committee meetings, I would just talk so fast about the quilt patterns, and the budgets, and all the publicity we needed to do. People would try to interrupt me, you know, they'd raise their hands or try to get a word in, but I just kept going. Stopping just felt completely impossible. 

It reminds me of when my sister, Brenda, used to talk on the telephone when we were teenagers. She had one of those long coiled cords on the kitchen phone, and she would stretch it all the way into the pantry so she could talk to her boyfriend in private. Our mother hated that. The cord would get all tangled up and stretched out of shape. Brenda finally ruined it completely by getting it caught in the pantry door hinge. My dad had to go to RadioShack to buy a replacement cord, and he made Brenda pay for it out of her babysitting money. She was so mad, she didn't speak to him for a week. Which was unusual for her, because Brenda was a talker, just like our Aunt Martha. Aunt Martha could talk the ear off a brass monkey, my dad used to say. She always wore these big, clunky clip-on earrings that jingled when she talked...

Oh, dear, what was I saying? Right, the meetings. Yes, I was talking so fast and just couldn't stop myself, no matter how much people tried to cut in.

Before you started feeling down, did you have a time that lasted at least four days where you felt so unusually good, energetic, or irritable that it was noticeable to others—even if it didn’t interfere with your work or relationships?

Well, it wasn't just a few days, it was... goodness, that whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months. Five whole months of feeling like that before everything just completely fell apart. 

It was right around the time we were trying to get the old train depot recognized as a historical landmark. We had to dig through all these county records from the 1800s. The archives room at the courthouse always smelled like old paper and floor wax. It reminded me of my elementary school library. Mrs. Gable was our librarian, and she used to keep a jar of butterscotch candies on her desk. The kind wrapped in that yellow cellophane that makes such a racket when you try to open it quietly during reading time. I tried to unwrap one during silent reading once, and she gave me such a stern look over her half-moon glasses. She always wore her glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck. My mother tried to wear one of those chains once, but it kept getting caught in her cardigan buttons. She loved cardigans, especially the ones with pearl buttons... 

But yes, five months. It was a solid five months of that energy before the crash happened.

Before you started feeling down, did you have a period that lasted at least four consecutive days where your mood was clearly elevated or irritable—so much so that other people noticed a change in you?

Well, yes, people definitely noticed. At first, I felt almost glowing, you know? Like every single idea I had for the quilt auction was just absolutely wonderful. But then... well, if anyone questioned me, like when Martha suggested we use a different batting for the baby quilts, I got so snappish. I acted like they were just standing in the way of progress. 

Martha always was a bit particular, though. She insists on using that 100% cotton batting, but I think the wool blend gives it a much nicer drape. We bought our batting from this little shop down on Main Street, right next to the bakery that makes those incredible bear claws. Oh, the bear claws there are to die for. They have this almond paste filling that isn't too sweet, and the icing... it flakes off all over your shirt when you eat it. My husband used to tease me because I'd always get powdered sugar on my black winter coat. He bought me that coat for our 25th anniversary. We went to Chicago that year, and it was so bitterly cold, the wind just whipped right off the lake. We walked all the way down the Magnificent Mile, and I thought my ears were going to freeze solid and snap right off. We had to duck into a department store just to thaw out...

But, oh, I'm sorry. You were asking about my mood, weren't you? Yes, I felt wonderful at first, but I did get awfully irritable if people didn't go along with my ideas.

In our committee meetings, I would just talk so fast about the quilt patterns, and the budgets, and all the publicity we needed to do. People would try to interrupt me, you know, they'd raise their hands or try to get a word in, but I just kept going. Stopping just felt completely impossible. 

It reminds me of when my sister, Brenda, used to talk on the telephone when we were teenagers. She had one of those long coiled cords on the kitchen phone, and she would stretch it all the way into the pantry so she could talk to her boyfriend in private. Our mother hated that. The cord would get all tangled up and stretched out of shape. Brenda finally ruined it completely by getting it caught in the pantry door hinge. My dad had to go to RadioShack to buy a replacement cord, and he made Brenda pay for it out of her babysitting money. She was so mad, she didn't speak to him for a week. Which was unusual for her, because Brenda was a talker, just like our Aunt Martha. Aunt Martha could talk the ear off a brass monkey, my dad used to say. She always wore these big, clunky clip-on earrings that jingled when she talked...

Oh, dear, what was I saying? Right, the meetings. Yes, I was talking so fast and just couldn't stop myself, no matter how much people tried to cut in.

inference.note: The patient described a distinct period of elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, and pressured speech before the current nine-month depressive episode, which supports the possibility of a prior manic episode. This maintains the candidate F31.3 (Bipolar disorder, current episode depressed, moderate). The chronic depressive symptoms also continue to support F33.3 (Recurrent depressive disorder, current episode depressed, moderate). No candidate ruled out this turn.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a manic or hypomanic episode that lasted at least four days, which would support a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (F31.3) rather than major depressive disorder (F33.3).
doctor.question: Before you started feeling down, did you have a time that lasted at least four days where you felt so unusually good, energetic, or irritable that it was noticeable to others—even if it didn’t interfere with your work or relationships?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: That overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months before everything fell apart.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the elevated, energetic, or irritable mood (at least four days). This corresponds to the duration of the manic/hypomanic episode.

patient.answer:
Well, it wasn't just a few days, it was... goodness, that whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months. Five whole months of feeling like that before everything just completely fell apart. 

It was right around the time we were trying to get the old train depot recognized as a historical landmark. We had to dig through all these county records from the 1800s. The archives room at the courthouse always smelled like old paper and floor wax. It reminded me of my elementary school library. Mrs. Gable was our librarian, and she used to keep a jar of butterscotch candies on her desk. The kind wrapped in that yellow cellophane that makes such a racket when you try to open it quietly during reading time. I tried to unwrap one during silent reading once, and she gave me such a stern look over her half-moon glasses. She always wore her glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck. My mother tried to wear one of those chains once, but it kept getting caught in her cardigan buttons. She loved cardigans, especially the ones with pearl buttons... 

But yes, five months. It was a solid five months of that energy before the crash happened.

inference.note: The patient reported a prior period lasting five months with elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, and irritability that was noticeable to others. This history of a prolonged manic episode rules out F33.3 (recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe without psychotic symptoms) and supports a diagnosis of F31.3 (bipolar disorder, current episode manic with mood congruent psychotic features or unspecified, depending on further inquiry).

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient had a period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood lasting at least 4 consecutive days, which is a key feature of a manic or hypomanic episode.
doctor.question: Before you started feeling down, did you have a period that lasted at least four consecutive days where your mood was clearly elevated or irritable—so much so that other people noticed a change in you?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: At first I felt almost glowing, like every idea I had was wonderful, but if anyone questioned me I got snappish and acted like they were standing in the way.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I experienced a period of elevated or irritable mood, which corresponds to the Elevated_Irritable_Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, people definitely noticed. At first, I felt almost glowing, you know? Like every single idea I had for the quilt auction was just absolutely wonderful. But then... well, if anyone questioned me, like when Martha suggested we use a different batting for the baby quilts, I got so snappish. I acted like they were just standing in the way of progress. 

Martha always was a bit particular, though. She insists on using that 100% cotton batting, but I think the wool blend gives it a much nicer drape. We bought our batting from this little shop down on Main Street, right next to the bakery that makes those incredible bear claws. Oh, the bear claws there are to die for. They have this almond paste filling that isn't too sweet, and the icing... it flakes off all over your shirt when you eat it. My husband used to tease me because I'd always get powdered sugar on my black winter coat. He bought me that coat for our 25th anniversary. We went to Chicago that year, and it was so bitterly cold, the wind just whipped right off the lake. We walked all the way down the Magnificent Mile, and I thought my ears were going to freeze solid and snap right off. We had to duck into a department store just to thaw out...

But, oh, I'm sorry. You were asking about my mood, weren't you? Yes, I felt wonderful at first, but I did get awfully irritable if people didn't go along with my ideas.

This confirms a bipolar I disorder with current episode depressed, moderate.
